raw: Act 2, Scene 2 — Capulet’s Garden
Enter Romeo.

speaker: ROMEO
raw: He jests at scars that never felt a wound.

sentences.en: He jokes about scars that never felt a wound.

raw: Juliet appears above at a window.

sentences.en: Juliet appears at a window above.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?
It is the east, and Juliet is the sun!
Arise fair sun and kill the envious moon,
Who is already sick and pale with grief,
That thou her maid art far more fair than she.
Be not her maid since she is envious;
Her vestal livery is but sick and green,
And none but fools do wear it; cast it off.
It is my lady, O it is my love!
O, that she knew she were!
She speaks, yet she says nothing. What of that?
Her eye discourses, I will answer it.
I am too bold, ’tis not to me she speaks.
Two of the fairest stars in all the heaven,
Having some business, do entreat her eyes
To twinkle in their spheres till they return.
What if her eyes were there, they in her head?
The brightness of her cheek would shame those stars,
As daylight doth a lamp; her eyes in heaven
Would through the airy region stream so bright
That birds would sing and think it were not night.
See how she leans her cheek upon her hand.
O that I were a glove upon that hand,
That I might touch that cheek.

sentences.en: Wait, what light breaks through that window over there?
It is the east, and Juliet is the sun!
Rise, fair sun, and kill the envious moon.
The moon is already sick and pale with grief.
She is jealous because you, her servant, are far more beautiful than she is.
Do not be her servant since she is jealous.
Her uniform of virginity is only sick and green.
Only fools wear it; throw it off.
It is my lady. Oh, it is my love!
Oh, if only she knew she was my love!
She speaks, yet she says nothing. What of that?
Her eyes communicate, and I will answer them.
I am too bold. She is not speaking to me.
Two of the most beautiful stars in all heaven have some business.
They ask her eyes to shine in their places until they return.
What if her eyes were there and those stars were in her head?
The brightness of her cheek would shame those stars, just as daylight shames a lamp.
Her eyes in heaven would shine so brightly through the air that birds would sing and think it was not night.
See how she leans her cheek on her hand.
Oh, I wish I were a glove on that hand.
Then I could touch that cheek.

speaker: JULIET
raw: Ay me.

sentences.en: Oh, dear me.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
She speaks.
O speak again bright angel, for thou art
As glorious to this night, being o’er my head,
As is a winged messenger of heaven
Unto the white-upturned wondering eyes
Of mortals that fall back to gaze on him
When he bestrides the lazy-puffing clouds
And sails upon the bosom of the air.

sentences.en: She speaks.
Oh, speak again, bright angel.
Up above my head tonight, you shine like an angel from heaven.
People fall back and stare up at such an angel with wide, wondering eyes.
He rides on the lazy, drifting clouds.
He sails through the air.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
O Romeo, Romeo, wherefore art thou Romeo?
Deny thy father and refuse thy name.
Or if thou wilt not, be but sworn my love,
And I’ll no longer be a Capulet.

sentences.en: Oh Romeo, Romeo, why are you Romeo?
Deny your father and refuse your name.
Or if you will not, just swear that you love me.
Then I will no longer be a Capulet.

speaker: ROMEO
raw: Shall I hear more, or shall I speak at this?

sentences.en: Shall I hear more, or shall I speak now?

speaker: JULIET
raw:
’Tis but thy name that is my enemy;
Thou art thyself, though not a Montague.
What’s Montague? It is nor hand nor foot,
Nor arm, nor face, nor any other part
Belonging to a man. O be some other name.
What’s in a name? That which we call a rose
By any other name would smell as sweet;
So Romeo would, were he not Romeo call’d,
Retain that dear perfection which he owes
Without that title. Romeo, doff thy name,
And for thy name, which is no part of thee,
Take all myself.

sentences.en: It is only your name that is my enemy.
You are yourself, even if you are not a Montague.
What is a Montague? It is not a hand or a foot.
It is not an arm, a face, or any other part of a man.
Oh, take some other name.
What is in a name?
A rose would smell as sweet if we called it by another name.
So Romeo would keep his perfection if he were not called Romeo.
He would have that quality without the title.
Romeo, throw off your name.
Instead of your name, which is no part of you, take all of me.

speaker: ROMEO

sentences.en: I accept your promise.
Just call me love, and I will be baptized again.
From now on, I will never be Romeo.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
What man art thou that, thus bescreen’d in night
So stumblest on my counsel?

sentences.en: What man are you?
You are hidden in the night.
How did you happen to overhear my private thoughts?

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
By a name
I know not how to tell thee who I am:
My name, dear saint, is hateful to myself,
Because it is an enemy to thee.
Had I it written, I would tear the word.

sentences.en: I do not know how to tell you who I am because of a name.
My name, dear saint, is hateful to me.
It is because it is an enemy to you.
If I had it written down, I would tear the word away.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
My ears have yet not drunk a hundred words
Of thy tongue’s utterance, yet I know the sound.
Art thou not Romeo, and a Montague?

sentences.en: I have not heard a hundred words from your mouth yet.
Still, I know the sound of your voice.
Are you not Romeo and a Montague?

speaker: ROMEO
raw: Neither, fair maid, if either thee dislike.

sentences.en: I am neither, beautiful girl, if you dislike either of those things.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
How cam’st thou hither, tell me, and wherefore?
The orchard walls are high and hard to climb,
And the place death, considering who thou art,
If any of my kinsmen find thee here.

sentences.en: Tell me how you came here and why.
The orchard walls are high and hard to climb.
Because of who you are, this place means death if any of my relatives find you here.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
With love’s light wings did I o’erperch these walls,
For stony limits cannot hold love out,
And what love can do, that dares love attempt:
Therefore thy kinsmen are no stop to me.

sentences.en: I flew over these walls on love's light wings.
Stone walls cannot keep love out.
Whatever love can do, love dares to try.
Therefore, your relatives are no stop to me.

speaker: JULIET
raw: If they do see thee, they will murder thee.

sentences.en: If they see you, they will murder you.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
Alack, there lies more peril in thine eye
Than twenty of their swords. Look thou but sweet,
And I am proof against their enmity.

sentences.en: Oh no, there is more danger in your eyes than in twenty of their swords.
Just look sweet, and I will be protected from their hatred.

speaker: JULIET
raw: I would not for the world they saw thee here.

sentences.en: I would not let them see you here for anything.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
I have night’s cloak to hide me from their eyes,
And but thou love me, let them find me here.
My life were better ended by their hate
Than death prorogued, wanting of thy love.

sentences.en: I have the night's cloak to hide me from their eyes.
And if you love me, let them find me here.
My life would be better ended by their hate than delayed without your love.

speaker: JULIET
raw: By whose direction found’st thou out this place?

sentences.en: Who told you how to find this place?

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
By love, that first did prompt me to enquire;
He lent me counsel, and I lent him eyes.
I am no pilot; yet wert thou as far
As that vast shore wash’d with the farthest sea,
I should adventure for such merchandise.

sentences.en: Love first prompted me to ask.
It gave me advice, and I gave it eyes.
I am not a pilot.
Yet if you were as far as that vast shore washed by the distant sea, I would take the risk for such a prize.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
Thou knowest the mask of night is on my face,
Else would a maiden blush bepaint my cheek
For that which thou hast heard me speak tonight.
Fain would I dwell on form, fain, fain deny
What I have spoke; but farewell compliment.
Dost thou love me? I know thou wilt say Ay,
And I will take thy word. Yet, if thou swear’st,
Thou mayst prove false. At lovers’ perjuries,
They say Jove laughs. O gentle Romeo,
If thou dost love, pronounce it faithfully.
Or if thou thinkest I am too quickly won,
I’ll frown and be perverse, and say thee nay,
So thou wilt woo. But else, not for the world.
In truth, fair Montague, I am too fond;
And therefore thou mayst think my ’haviour light:
But trust me, gentleman, I’ll prove more true
Than those that have more cunning to be strange.
I should have been more strange, I must confess,
But that thou overheard’st, ere I was ’ware,
My true-love passion; therefore pardon me,
And not impute this yielding to light love,
Which the dark night hath so discovered.

sentences.en: You know the mask of night is on my face.
Otherwise, a girl's blush would color my cheek for what you heard me say tonight.
I would gladly act properly and politely.
I would gladly, gladly deny what I said.
But I give up polite behavior.
Do you love me?
I know you will say yes, and I will take your word.
Yet, if you swear it, you might prove false.
They say Jove laughs at lovers' broken promises.
Oh gentle Romeo, if you love me, say it faithfully.
Or if you think I am too easily won, I will frown and be stubborn.
I will say no, so that you will try to win my love.
But otherwise, not for the world.
In truth, fair Montague, I love you too much.
Therefore you might think my behavior is not serious.
But trust me, gentleman, I will prove more true than those who are skilled at pretending not to care.
I should have been more distant, I must confess.
But you overheard my true love passion before I was aware.
Therefore forgive me.
Do not blame my quick yes on a light love; the dark night revealed it.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
Lady, by yonder blessed moon I vow,
That tips with silver all these fruit-tree tops,—

sentences.en: Lady, by that blessed moon over there I vow, that tips all these fruit-tree tops with silver—

speaker: JULIET
raw:
O swear not by the moon, th’inconstant moon,
That monthly changes in her circled orb,
Lest that thy love prove likewise variable.

sentences.en: Oh, do not swear by the moon.
The moon is always changing.
It changes every month in its circle.
I do not want your love to change like that.

speaker: ROMEO
raw: What shall I swear by?

sentences.en: What should I swear by?

speaker: JULIET
raw:
Do not swear at all.
Or if thou wilt, swear by thy gracious self,
Which is the god of my idolatry,
And I’ll believe thee.

sentences.en: Do not swear at all.
Or if you want to, swear by your gracious self.
You are the god of my worship.
Then I will believe you.

speaker: ROMEO
raw: If my heart’s dear love,—

sentences.en: If my heart's dear love—

speaker: JULIET
raw:
Well, do not swear. Although I joy in thee,
I have no joy of this contract tonight;
It is too rash, too unadvis’d, too sudden,
Too like the lightning, which doth cease to be
Ere one can say “It lightens.” Sweet, good night.
This bud of love, by summer’s ripening breath,
May prove a beauteous flower when next we meet.
Good night, good night. As sweet repose and rest
Come to thy heart as that within my breast.

sentences.en: Well, do not swear.
Although I find joy in you, I have no joy in this contract tonight.
It is too rash, not thought through, and too sudden.
It is like lightning, which stops before one can say 'It lightens'.
Good night.
With summer's warm breath, this bud of love may be a beautiful flower when we next meet.
Good night, good night.
May the same sweet peace that is in my heart come to your heart.

speaker: ROMEO
raw: O wilt thou leave me so unsatisfied?

sentences.en: Oh, will you leave me so unsatisfied?

speaker: JULIET
raw: What satisfaction canst thou have tonight?

sentences.en: What satisfaction can you have tonight?

speaker: ROMEO
raw: Th’exchange of thy love’s faithful vow for mine.

sentences.en: The exchange of your faithful vow for mine.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
I gave thee mine before thou didst request it;
And yet I would it were to give again.

sentences.en: I gave you mine before you asked for it.
And yet I wish I could give it again.

speaker: ROMEO
raw: Would’st thou withdraw it? For what purpose, love?

sentences.en: Would you take it back?
For what reason, my love?

speaker: JULIET
raw:
But to be frank and give it thee again.
And yet I wish but for the thing I have;
My bounty is as boundless as the sea,
My love as deep; the more I give to thee,
The more I have, for both are infinite.
I hear some noise within. Dear love, adieu.

sentences.en: I want to be generous and give it to you again.
Yet I only want the thing I already have.
My generosity is as boundless as the sea, and my love is just as deep.
The more I give to you, the more I have because both are infinite.
I hear some noise from inside.
My dear love, goodbye.

raw: Nurse calls within.

sentences.en: The Nurse calls from inside.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
Anon, good Nurse!—Sweet Montague be true.
Stay but a little, I will come again.

sentences.en: Coming, good Nurse!
Sweet Montague, be true.
Wait just a little, for I will come back again.

raw: Exit.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
O blessed, blessed night. I am afeard,
Being in night, all this is but a dream,
Too flattering sweet to be substantial.

sentences.en: Oh, blessed, blessed night.
I am afraid.
Since it is night, all of this might be a dream.
It is too sweet to be real.

raw: Enter Juliet above.

sentences.en: Juliet comes back to the window.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
Three words, dear Romeo, and good night indeed.
If that thy bent of love be honourable,
Thy purpose marriage, send me word tomorrow,
By one that I’ll procure to come to thee,
Where and what time thou wilt perform the rite,
And all my fortunes at thy foot I’ll lay
And follow thee my lord throughout the world.

sentences.en: Three words, dear Romeo, and then really good night.
If your love is honorable and your plan is marriage, send me word tomorrow.
I will find someone to come to you so that person can tell me where and at what time we will marry.
I will give all my fortunes at your feet and follow you as my lord throughout the world.

speaker: NURSE
raw: Madam.

sentences.en: Madam.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
I come, anon.— But if thou meanest not well,
I do beseech thee,—

sentences.en: I am coming right away.
But if you do not mean well, I beg you—

speaker: NURSE
raw: Madam.

sentences.en: Madam.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
By and by I come—
To cease thy strife and leave me to my grief.
Tomorrow will I send.

sentences.en: I will come in a moment.
Stop trying, and leave me to my sadness.
I will send word tomorrow.

speaker: ROMEO
raw: So thrive my soul,—

sentences.en: As I hope for heaven—

speaker: JULIET
raw: A thousand times good night.

sentences.en: Good night a thousand times.

raw: Exit.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
A thousand times the worse, to want thy light.
Love goes toward love as schoolboys from their books,
But love from love, towards school with heavy looks.

sentences.en: It is a thousand times worse without your light.
Love goes toward love as happily as schoolboys leave their books.
But love leaves love as sadly as schoolboys go to school.

raw: Retiring slowly.

sentences.en: Romeo moves away slowly.

raw: Re-enter Juliet, above.

sentences.en: Juliet comes back to the window.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
Hist! Romeo, hist! O for a falconer’s voice
To lure this tassel-gentle back again.
Bondage is hoarse and may not speak aloud,
Else would I tear the cave where Echo lies,
And make her airy tongue more hoarse than mine
With repetition of my Romeo’s name.

sentences.en: Psst! Romeo, psst!
Oh, I wish for a falconer's voice.
I want to call this male falcon back again.
I am not free and cannot speak loudly.
If I could speak loudly, I would destroy the cave where Echo lives.
I would make her thin voice even more hoarse than mine.
I would do it by making her repeat my Romeo's name over and over.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
It is my soul that calls upon my name.
How silver-sweet sound lovers’ tongues by night,
Like softest music to attending ears.

sentences.en: It is my soul that calls my name.
How sweet lovers' voices sound at night.
They sound like soft music to the ears of those listening.

speaker: JULIET
raw: Romeo.

sentences.en: Romeo.

speaker: ROMEO
raw: My dear?

sentences.en: My dear?

speaker: JULIET
raw:
What o’clock tomorrow
Shall I send to thee?

sentences.en: What time tomorrow should I send for you?

speaker: ROMEO
raw: By the hour of nine.

sentences.en: At nine o'clock.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
I will not fail. ’Tis twenty years till then.
I have forgot why I did call thee back.

sentences.en: I will not fail.
It is twenty years until then.
I have forgotten why I called you back.

speaker: ROMEO
raw: Let me stand here till thou remember it.

sentences.en: Let me stand here until you remember it.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
I shall forget, to have thee still stand there,
Remembering how I love thy company.

sentences.en: I will keep forgetting, so that you stay there.
I will only remember how much I love being with you.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
And I’ll still stay, to have thee still forget,
Forgetting any other home but this.

sentences.en: And I will stay, so that you keep forgetting.
I will forget any home but this one.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
’Tis almost morning; I would have thee gone,
And yet no farther than a wanton’s bird,
That lets it hop a little from her hand,
Like a poor prisoner in his twisted gyves,
And with a silk thread plucks it back again,
So loving-jealous of his liberty.

sentences.en: It is almost morning.
I want you to go.
But no farther than a spoiled child's pet bird.
She lets it hop a little from her hand, like a poor prisoner in chains.
Then she pulls it back again with a silk thread.
She loves it too much to let it be free.

speaker: ROMEO
raw: I would I were thy bird.

sentences.en: I wish I were your bird.

speaker: JULIET
raw:
Sweet, so would I:
Yet I should kill thee with much cherishing.
Good night, good night. Parting is such sweet sorrow
That I shall say good night till it be morrow.

sentences.en: Sweet, I would too.
But I would kill you if I held you too closely.
Good night, good night.
Parting is such sweet sorrow.
I could keep saying good night until morning.

raw: Exit.

speaker: ROMEO
raw:
Sleep dwell upon thine eyes, peace in thy breast.
Would I were sleep and peace, so sweet to rest.
Hence will I to my ghostly Sire’s cell,
His help to crave and my dear hap to tell.

sentences.en: May sleep fall on your eyes and peace be in your breast.
I wish I were sleep and peace to give you such a sweet rest.
I must go now to my priest's small room.
I will ask for his help and tell him my good fortune.

raw: Exit.
